payload.throughline: Extract a passage-bounded invariant, map its roles and relations into a supplied context, infer a passage-consistent result, and recognize the same structure beneath different imagery.

Objective: Extract a reusable passage framework by naming the principle, relation, perspective, constraint, or paradigm that remains stable when topic details change.
Helpful prior CARS context may support passage reading, but this lesson itself teaches the abstraction move: separate what the passage is about from the relation it uses to reason.
A topic label names the subject; a transferable framework states how elements relate, what constraint governs them, or what perspective organizes the author’s judgment.
Build the invariant from passage evidence only. Compress repeated claims into a conditional or relational statement that could survive replacement of the passage’s nouns.
Do not import an outside theory to make the framework more impressive. The usable abstraction must remain traceable to the author’s own claims and examples.
Use a two-column extraction: changing details on the left, stable relation on the right. If replacing the nouns destroys the statement, it is probably a topic summary rather than an invariant.

I ask what repeated judgment links the examples. I reject answers that merely name the domain, quote one illustration, or add a theory the author never supplied. Then I phrase the stable relation with roles and a verb.

Synthetic passage: a designer praises old markets not for their brickwork but because sellers can continually rearrange stalls in response to neighbors. The topic is markets; the invariant is that adaptable shared arrangements preserve communal function.
That invariant could map to a classroom, software team, or public institution without carrying market vocabulary with it.
Guided practice: mark the repeated evaluative relation, then distinguish it from the passage topic and examples.
Less support: compress a fresh paragraph into one passage-bounded relational statement.
Independent practice: identify the invariant without importing outside facts or theory.
Boundary: “the passage discusses museums” is a topic summary. “Acknowledging uncertainty preserves intellectual honesty” is a usable framework only when the passage repeatedly supports that relation.

Changed-task exit: preserve the governed relation while selecting or applying it in a substantively different situation.
Repair topic-only extraction by underlining repeated verbs of judgment—enables, limits, preserves, distorts—and naming the roles on each side of that relation.

Repair framework inflation by deleting every concept not warranted by the passage, then restating the smallest relation that explains all cited examples.
Fresh re-entry checks only the failed changed-task function in a new context and does not reuse the exposed answer.
A transferable framework is passage-derived, relational, and noun-replaceable. It is neither a topic label nor an external theory.

Objective: Map the relevant roles, relations, and constraints of a fixed passage framework onto a question-specified new context without changing the framework.
The prior microcycle extracted an invariant. This one keeps that invariant fixed and builds an explicit source-role to target-role correspondence before inferring anything.
A valid mapping pairs roles by function, not by shared vocabulary. Identify who or what occupies each source role and preserve the direction of the relation between them.
Use only target facts supplied by the question. Outside knowledge and surface resemblance can distract from a clean role-and-relation mapping.
After mapping, restate the source relation with target labels. If the relation changes direction, gains a new premise, or drops a constraint, the framework was changed rather than applied.
Build a three-row map: source role, target role, preserved relation. Check every arrow before drawing the passage-consistent implication.

I ignore repeated nouns and ask what each element does. Then I test whether the target relation has the same direction and constraint. A mapping with similar imagery but reversed causal roles is invalid.
Source framework: reversible sketches let a craft learner test choices before a permanent cut. Target context: a programmer uses a disposable prototype before altering production code.
The sketch maps to the prototype, the permanent cut to the production change, and low-cost revision to safe testing. The relation is preserved without requiring the domains to look alike.
Guided practice: fill source role, target role, and preserved relation before choosing an implication.
Less support: map roles by function while ignoring repeated surface words.
Independent practice: apply a fixed relation to a supplied context without adding outside facts.
Boundary: mapping “garden” to “garden” because the nouns match is surface-only. Mapping diversity that buffers failure to portfolio diversity that buffers loss preserves a relation.

Changed-task exit: preserve the governed relation while selecting or applying it in a substantively different situation.
Repair role confusion with a correspondence table. For every source element, state its function before selecting a target element with the same function.

Map functions, preserve arrow direction and constraints, then infer. Shared words are optional; a fixed relation is not.

Objective: Infer an author’s likely response or a passage-consistent outcome in a specified hypothetical by applying the author model and passage constraints.
The source framework and target mapping are now available. This microcycle uses them to project a bounded response rather than predict personal preference or real-world likelihood.
Build an author model from explicit judgments, concessions, and repeated priorities. The hypothetical answer must preserve that model even when the new case is unfamiliar.
Distinguish “what would probably happen in the world” from “what follows if the passage’s framework governs.” Only the second is passage-consistent inference.
Use the smallest warranted change. Do not make the author absolute when the passage was qualified, and do not erase a constraint because the hypothetical is vivid.
Use a three-step projection: author priority, hypothetical feature, constrained response. Every inference arrow must be backed by a passage claim.
I phrase the author’s priority before reading the options. Then I ask which choice preserves both that priority and any concession. I reject answers based on my own preference or outside probability.
Synthetic author model: metrics are useful prompts for inquiry but become dangerous when treated as substitutes for judgment.
Hypothetical: a dashboard flags an unusual result. The passage-consistent response is to investigate the anomaly with contextual judgment, not ignore all metrics or obey the number automatically.
Guided practice: state the author priority and limiting concession before projecting a response.
Less support: infer a response while preserving qualified rather than absolute language.
Independent practice: choose a passage-consistent result without substituting personal prediction.
Boundary: “most organizations would choose this” is outside likelihood. “Given the author’s stated priority, the organization would choose this” is a passage-model inference.

Repair stance drift by citing one author priority and one concession, then eliminate any response that violates either.

Repair outside-likelihood reasoning by adding the phrase “if the passage framework governs” and deriving only the result licensed by that condition.

Project from the author model through the supplied hypothetical, preserve qualifications, and keep real-world likelihood outside the inference.

Objective: Identify a fundamental relation shared by passage content and a superficially different case, including figurative-to-literal translation.
The earlier mapping microcycle paired roles in an explicitly supplied framework. This one must first detect which relation is fundamental before mapping it across unlike surfaces.
A structural analogy preserves roles, relation direction, and relevant constraints. Shared topic, imagery, or vocabulary is neither necessary nor sufficient.
Translate figurative language into a literal relational skeleton before comparing options. “Lens,” for example, may mean selective amplification plus narrowed field rather than optical equipment.
Test candidate analogies for both positive correspondence and disanalogy. One matching noun cannot compensate for a reversed causal arrow.
Reduce both cases to role–relation–role diagrams. Compare arrows and constraints first; restore domain labels only after the structural match is established.
I paraphrase the source without imagery, then do the same for each target. I select the target with the same functional arrows and reject cases that share scenery but not structure.
Source: roots connected through fungi move nutrients from resource-rich plants toward stressed neighbors. Skeleton: a distributed network redirects surplus from strong nodes to vulnerable nodes.
Target: experienced teams share expertise through a peer network with teams facing a new problem. The domains differ, but the support relation is preserved.
Guided practice: strip imagery from the source and compare role–relation diagrams.
Less support: select the target with matching arrows despite different vocabulary.
Independent practice: translate a figurative relation into a literal structural match.
Boundary: two passages about rivers may have no structural analogy; a river bend that slows flow may instead match a deliberative pause that surfaces overlooked material.

Changed-task exit: preserve the governed relation while selecting or applying it in a substantively different situation.
